# "Disaster is Rarely as Pervasive as it Seems from Recorded Accounts" — Barbara Tuchman: A Discussion

## Introduction

In the introduction to her 1978 book *A Distant Mirror*, Tuchman identified a historical phenomenon she termed "Tuchman's Law." The law states simply: *"Disaster is rarely as pervasive as it seems from recorded accounts."* The fact of being on the record makes it appear continuous and ubiquitous, whereas it is more likely to have been sporadic both in time and place. Besides, the persistence of the normal is usually greater than the effect of the disturbance, as we know from our own times. This deceptively simple observation cuts to the heart of how we understand history, media, and human experience. To discuss it fully, we must examine the mechanisms that generate this illusion of universal catastrophe, consider powerful case studies, and then also weigh the argument's limits — for some disasters *are* genuinely pervasive.

---

## I. The Core of Tuchman's Argument: Recording Creates Distortion

Tuchman's insight is fundamentally about **representation and selection**. She formulated her law as follows: "The fact of being reported multiplies the apparent extent of any deplorable development by five- to tenfold." This is not a claim that disasters do not happen or do not matter; it is a claim about how the act of recording disaster systematically exaggerates its universality.

Tuchman herself illustrated the point with a brilliantly mundane example drawn from contemporary life: after absorbing the news of today, one expects to face a world consisting entirely of strikes, crimes, power failures, broken water mains, stalled trains, school shutdowns, muggers, drug addicts, neo-Nazis, and rapists. The fact is that one can come home in the evening — on a lucky day — without having encountered more than one or two of these phenomena. The gap between the *recorded* world and the *lived* world, she suggests, is vast — and historians who fail to appreciate this gap will systematically misread the past.

---

## II. The Problem of Selective Recording (Survivorship Bias)

One of the most powerful mechanisms behind Tuchman's Law is what modern analysts call **survivorship bias**. Survivor bias is when we only look at the data of those who succeed and exclude those who fail. Applied to historical records, this means that we read the accounts of people alarmed enough to write them down — the churchman terrified by plague, the chronicler horrified by war — while the vast majority of people who experienced events quietly and unremarkably left no record at all.

In historical and political studies, survivorship bias is also often discussed in the context of research relying on statistical methods. It also appears in discussions concerning critical approaches to written sources.

A classic non-historical example of survivorship bias illuminates this brilliantly: WWII bombers were the subject of a classic study that suffered from survivorship bias. Researchers began analyzing US bombers returning to their bases to see which areas were damaged so that they could be further reinforced. By the very nature of the study, the planes being studied were "survivors," and it was realized that the areas that hadn't been hit were more worthy of study. Planes that didn't make it back might well have been hit in those places and crashed as a consequence. By studying only the surviving planes, the analysis suffered from incomplete and misleading data. The same logic applies to historical accounts: the records that survive are not a random sample — they are the records of disruption, complaint, and crisis.

---

## III. Case Study: The Black Death

The Black Death offers perhaps the most powerful illustration of Tuchman's Law in action, not least because it is the central disaster of *A Distant Mirror* itself. The Black Death epidemic killed about half the population of England, and many historical changes have been ascribed to it. But we still know surprisingly little about how the epidemic actually affected people's daily lives.

Tuchman's Law would predict that despite the horror of the chronicle accounts, much of ordinary life continued with surprising resilience. Recent bioarchaeological research has confirmed precisely this. Although the epidemic killed millions, no dramatic changes in skeletal indicators of health and lifestyle are directly ascribable to the epidemic. Most indicators either remained stable, or changed in response to other known historical trends. Traumatic though the plague was, it did not transform medieval people's health and lifeways radically.

Indeed, there were many things that apparently didn't change much. The basic structure of medieval society and politics remained remarkably stable, and changes in literature, art, architecture and religion were subtle at best. It is possible that the plague killed huge numbers of people, but didn't change structural elements of medieval society dramatically.

The documentary record itself shows the distorting lens of catastrophe. In its entry on the Black Death, a chronicle from the English city of Rochester includes among its harrowing details a seemingly trivial lament that aristocrats had to pay triple wages to field workers, or even perform manual labor themselves. Curiously, the documentary record, which provides ample evidence that workers did demand and receive higher wages, contains in contrast scant evidence that "worthies" ever dirtied their hands with fieldwork. The chronicler's outrage is recorded; the quiet pragmatism of daily survival is not.

---

## IV. The Modern Parallel: Media Negativity Bias

Tuchman's Law translates seamlessly into the modern media landscape. The tendency to select negative information in journalistic selection processes advocates an increased misrepresentation or exaggeration of negative incidents compared to reality.

In their overly negative and event-driven reporting, news media are commonly found to portray a biased reality. Overall, good news is seen as synonymous with no news, as negativity is believed to be more attention-grabbing and thereby garners the highest audience ratings and number of clicks. In this predominant focus on negativity, sensational and exceptional events often gain disproportionate news attention.

Crucially, the infrequency of incidents paradoxically explains the level of news coverage, and therewith isolated and negative events are mistakenly presented as daily reality. A plane crash — extraordinarily rare — receives far more coverage than the millions of safe flights that occur every year. Numerous studies empirically demonstrate that media's distortion of reality and negativity bias can have a profound effect on public opinion.

This psychological dynamic also feeds back into how we process information: negativity bias refers to the fact that humans focus on negative events, information, or emotions more than their positive counterparts. Tuchman's Law is therefore not merely a problem of historical records — it is a problem rooted in human cognition itself.

Tuchman's Law has been defined as a psychological principle of "perceptual readiness" or "subjective probability" and one that is a useful guide in how to align with our subjective misunderstanding of the world's dangers fueled by television and other media, where random but rare acts of violence seem more prevalent than the higher rates of harm that stem, for example, from financial fraud and corporate or government decisions.

---

## V. The Role of "Normal Persistence"

A key element of Tuchman's thinking is that human society has a remarkable capacity for **normative resilience** — a tendency to continue ordinary life even amid upheaval. The fact of being on the record makes disruption appear continuous and ubiquitous, whereas it is more likely to have been sporadic both in time and place. Besides, the persistence of the normal is usually greater than the effect of the disturbance.

This observation is supported by research into epidemic history beyond the Black Death.
